title: Genetic Engineering and Evolution Across Biological Systems: A Structured Review of the Origin, Transmission, and Population Fate of Engineered Variation
content: Genetic engineering deliberately alters biological material, but the transmission, spread, and continued function of engineered variation remain subject to evolutionary processes. This structured narrative review compares engineered crops, insect gene drives, and engineered microbes through an origin–transmission–population fate framework, distinguishing control at the sequence, inheritance, and ecological levels. Crop studies document pollen-mediated gene flow, multi-year transgene persistence in a weedy relative, and pest resistance alongside regional pest suppression. Gene-drive studies demonstrate biased inheritance and collapse of particular cage populations, while resistance and ecological heterogeneity constrain extrapolation to other settings. Microbial studies show that construct burden, genetic exchange, and selection can undermine intended functions despite successful initial engineering and host colonization. Together, these findings distinguish molecular precision from control over inheritance, population persistence, and ecological outcomes: initial technical success does not establish lasting practical benefit. The review maps research designs to the claims they can support and identifies difficulties in comparison across systems, interpretation of evidence, and observation over relevant evolutionary time scales. Priorities include multigenerational monitoring, comparable measures of genetic persistence and functional stability, and staged, context-sensitive evaluation. The framework connects molecular intervention with population processes and clarifies the evidence needed for biosafety and governance decisions.
